notes.meaning: Luke opens by reminding Theophilus of his first book, the Gospel of Luke. That Gospel recorded all the things Jesus began to do and teach while on earth. The book of Acts shows that Jesus is still working today through the Holy Spirit and his church.

Jesus ended his earthly work when God took him up into heaven. Before ascending, he gave important instructions to the apostles he had picked. Even as the risen Lord, Jesus gave these commands through the power of the Holy Spirit, setting an example for all believers.

Jesus showed himself alive to his apostles over forty days after his death on the cross. He gave many clear proofs that left no room for doubt, such as eating with them and letting them touch his body. During this time, he continued teaching them about God's kingdom.

Jesus gathered the apostles together and ordered them not to rush out of Jerusalem. Instead, they had to wait for the gift God the Father had promised to send. They could not do effective work for God until this divine help arrived.

John the Baptist had dipped people in water to show they were turning from sin, but Jesus promised something far greater. In a few days, Jesus would baptize his followers with the Holy Spirit, plunging them into God's life and power. This promised gift was Christ's own work to prepare them for ministry.

differ.view: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is an empowering work that usually happens after a person is saved and is accompanied by speaking in tongues.
Baptism with the Holy Spirit takes place at the moment of salvation, joining the new believer to the body of Christ once for all.

notes.meaning: The disciples asked Jesus if he was about to set up a political kingdom and free Israel from Roman rule. They still expected the Messiah to bring immediate earthly power to their nation. Jesus wanted to lift their thoughts from worldly politics to God's worldwide spiritual kingdom.

differ.view: Jesus did not reject a future earthly kingdom for Israel, but only told the apostles that the time for that national restoration was God's secret.

notes.meaning: Jesus told the disciples that the Father alone has set the dates and seasons by his own authority. Human beings are not meant to know the exact schedule of God's future plans. Believers should trust God's timing instead of trying to figure out prophetic dates.

Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would come upon the disciples with power to make them bold witnesses. They would tell people about Jesus in their home city of Jerusalem, across Judea and Samaria, and all the way to the ends of the earth. The Holy Spirit was the real engine behind this worldwide mission.

Right after Jesus finished speaking, he was lifted up into the air while the apostles watched. A cloud received him and hid him from their eyes. This visible departure showed that his earthly visits were finished and that he had returned to his glorious place in heaven.

The apostles kept staring up into the sky as Jesus disappeared from view. Suddenly, two angels appearing as men in bright white clothing stood right next to them. Their white clothing showed the pure glory of heaven.

The angels asked the apostles why they were still staring into the sky. They promised that this same Jesus will return in the same visible, physical way he had just left. This sure promise gave the disciples comfort and turned their minds toward their mission.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Until Christ returns visibly at the end of time, he appoints visible leaders who govern the church as successors of the apostles.

notes.meaning: The disciples obeyed Jesus and walked back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives. That walk was a Sabbath day's journey, which was about three-quarters of a mile—the legal limit a Jew could travel on the rest day. They returned to the city filled with joy and ready to obey.

The eleven apostles went upstairs to the upper room where they were staying. Luke lists each apostle by name to show who remained after Judas deserted them. This quiet room gave them a private and safe place to meet and seek God.

All the believers joined together in constant, united prayer. Devout women, Jesus' mother Mary, and his brothers were praying alongside the apostles. Jesus' brothers had not believed in him during his earthly ministry, but his resurrection brought them to saving faith.

During the days before Pentecost, Peter stood up before the group of about one hundred and twenty believers. As the natural spokesman for the apostles, he took the lead to guide the church. He knew that an important matter needed to be handled while they waited for the Spirit.

Peter pointed out that the Old Testament Scriptures had to come true concerning Judas. Hundreds of years earlier, the Holy Spirit had spoken through King David about a close companion who would betray God's servant. Judas did exactly that when he led the enemies who arrested Jesus.

Judas had been fully counted as one of the twelve apostles. Jesus had chosen him and given him an active share in the work of preaching and healing. His betrayal was shocking, but it left an empty position that needed to be filled.

The blood money Judas received for betraying Jesus was used to buy a field, where his body fell and split open. Everyone in Jerusalem heard about his awful end and named that place Akeldama, which means Field of Blood. Luke adds these verses as an explanation so his readers understand what happened to the traitor.

Peter quoted from the book of Psalms to show that Judas's ruin and replacement were part of God's plan. Scripture foretold that the traitor's home would become deserted and that another person should take his position of leadership. This gave the church clear biblical guidance to choose a new apostle.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Peter's quotation about taking another man's office shows that apostolic offices continue through successors, laying the foundation for bishops.

notes.meaning: Peter explained the strict standards needed for anyone replacing Judas. The candidate had to be a man who had traveled with Jesus throughout his whole earthly ministry, from John's baptism to the ascension. His main job would be to stand with the eleven as an eyewitness of Jesus' resurrection.

The believers nominated two men who met all the requirements: Joseph Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. Both men had faithfully followed Jesus from the start and seen him alive after he rose. The community recognized both as worthy candidates for the sacred office.

Before making a choice, the entire assembly prayed together. They addressed God as the Lord who knows every person's secret thoughts and motives. They asked him to show plainly which of the two men he had chosen for the work.

The church asked God to place the chosen man into the ministry and apostleship that Judas had walked away from. Judas had fallen into sin and gone to the place of punishment he chose for himself. The new apostle was to step into that empty office and serve faithfully.

The believers cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias. Casting lots was an Old Testament way of leaving a hard decision entirely in God's hands. Matthias was then counted as an apostle alongside the eleven.

differ.view: The disciples acted too quickly in casting lots, and God's true choice to fill the twelfth apostolic seat was the apostle Paul.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The selection of Matthias to succeed Judas is the first historical example of apostolic succession, where the apostles pass their office to new leaders.
